scenes.name: Sugar Hill Records y Rapper’s Delight
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sylvia Robinson, la «madre del hip hop», venía del R&B: Little Sylvia, el dúo Mickey & Sylvia («Love Is Strange», 1956), la producción del «It’s Gonna Work Out Fine» de Ike & Tina, el sello All Platinum con su marido Joe (con supuestos lazos mafiosos) y su propio éxito «Pillow Talk» (1973). Arruinada, vio a Lovebug Starski en Harlem World en 1979 y quiso grabar aquello; con Morris Levy fundaron Sugar Hill. Su hijo la llevó a una pizzería de Nueva Jersey donde Big Bank Hank, mánager de los Cold Crush, hizo una audición en su coche junto a Master Gee y Wonder Mike: la Sugarhill Gang. Sobre una recreación de «Good Times» de Chic grabaron quince minutos de rimas que una radio de St. Louis, WESL, se atrevió a poner: «Rapper’s Delight» inundó el mundo en otoño de 1979, dejó en anécdota el «King Tim III» de Fatback y demostró que el hip hop era negocio. En el Bronx sonaba a imitación higienizada: Hank rapeaba las rimas de Grandmaster Caz («I’m the C-A-S-AN, the O-V-A»), un estribillo de Hollywood y una frase de Rahiem; «hizo retroceder el hip hop cinco años» (Charlie Chase). Para Kool Moe Dee, sin Sugar Hill quizá no habría industria. La casa no pagaba bien a sus artistas, y su banda (Skip Alexander, Doug Wimbish, Duke Bootee) tocaba los temas. En Harlem, Bobby Robinson y su sello Enjoy ficharon a Flash, los Funky 4 + 1 y los Treacherous Three.

scenes.name: Chic
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La cima de la banda de baile neoyorquina: el bajista Bernard Edwards y el guitarrista Nile Rodgers pulieron el espíritu soul y los acordes jazzísticos del funk duro para el sonido elegante de la jet set disco, con riffs ajustados, voces sencillas y un groove con el funk justo para respirar. Vestían a la última y alejaron la imagen de la banda negra de los freaks tribales y guerreros espaciales. «Le Freak» (1978) inició la moda de las canciones «freak», que acabó degradando a las mujeres («I Need a Freak», «The Freaks Come Out at Night»); «Good Times» (1979), seis semanas número 1 soul, fue la base sobre la que la Sugarhill Gang grabó «Rapper’s Delight»: la mayor aportación del disco a la historia fue darle al hip hop su punto de partida.

scenes.name: Pop de club de los ochenta
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: La disco sale del gueto: apogeo de los extended mixes y del DJ remezclador (John Morales, Shep Pettibone, Jellybean, Kevorkian) que convierte cualquier estilo en dance hit. Grace Jones, Madonna —surgida de las discotecas con Jellybean y Nile Rodgers— y Prince, «la gran fuerza creadora de los ochenta», un artista electrónico para los músicos de Detroit.

podcast.title: Producer for Madonna's "Angel" (1985)
podcast.body: The legendary Nile Rodgers produced Madonna's synth pop track "Angel," which was her take on New Wave sound and peaked at number five. "Angel, Madonna's take on New Wave's synth pop, produced by the legendary Nile Rogers, was itself a pretty great song."

podcast.title: Mid-90s Overdose and Eight Flatlines
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, renowned producer and musician Nile Rodgers was a severe abuser of drugs and alcohol, often partying with Robert Downey Jr. A particularly intense period of cocaine and alcohol use led him to the hospital, where he flatlined eight times. He was legally dead, and doctors were completing paperwork when he unexpectedly started breathing on his own. "He ended up in hospital where he flatlined eight times. He'd actually been legally dead, and the doctors were filling up the paperwork. When he suddenly started breathing again on his own, he was that far gone."

xref.title: Around the World (1997) – Goal Was to Sound Like Chic; Repeated 144 Times; Declared One of the Most Repetitive Songs Ever
xref.body: "Around the World" was designed to sound like Chic (Nile Rodgers's disco-era band). The song has five instruments and a robotic voice saying "Around the World." In the original version, the phrase is repeated 144 times (80 times in the short edit). A scientific analysis of music declared it one of the most repetitive songs ever released — and that is its genius, as repetition is what creates the sensation of losing yourself in music. "A scientific analysis of music declared this to be one of the most repetitive songs ever released. And that is its genius."

xref.title: Collaboration with Nile Rodgers
xref.body: For his 1983 album "Let's Dance," David Bowie collaborated with Nile Rodgers, known as the driving force behind Chic, one of the notable disco bands of the late 1970s. This collaboration allowed Bowie to create a sound that blended alternative, post disco, and alt dance elements. "He was produced by Nile Rogers, the guy behind Sheik, one of the better disco bands in the late 1970s."

xref.title: Session and Touring Musician
xref.body: Collins was a highly sought-after guitarist, frequently called upon by producer Nile Rodgers for recordings with his clients, including Madonna. She also toured with George Clinton and P-Funk and served as the studio and touring guitarist for the Thompson Twins during their peak in the mid-1980s. "For that, she was a go-to person for guitarist and producer Nile Rogers, who had her play on many records for his clients, including Madonna."
